title: Forward / reverse starter with interlocks
summary: Reverse a motor by swapping two phases, and stop the two contactors ever closing together.

why.text:
The return conveyor **CV-7** at the fictional Riverside plant must run both ways: forward to feed crates, reverse to clear a jam. That needs two contactors, one for each direction.

If both ever close at the same time, two phases are joined straight through the contactors. That is a short circuit with an arc inside the panel. Your job is to make that impossible.

cards.title: Reversing a three-phase motor
cards.text:
The direction of a three-phase motor depends on the [[phase sequence]] at U1, V1, W1. Swap **any two** phases and it runs the other way.

A reversing starter has two contactors: **KM1 forward** passes L1, L2, L3 straight through; **KM2 reverse** swaps two of them (here L1 and L3). Their outputs join and go through one overload to the motor.

cards.title: Why both must never close
cards.text:
Look at the power circuit: the output of KM1 pole 1 and KM2 pole 1 are joined. With KM1 in, that point is L1. With KM2 in, it is L3. If both close, L1 and L3 are joined through the contactors: a phase-to-phase short circuit.

The protective device should trip, but the arc can damage the contactors and anyone near an open panel.

cards.title: The electrical interlock
cards.text:
Each coil circuit goes through the **other** contactor's [[NC]] auxiliary contact (21-22):
- KM1 coil is fed through **KM2 21-22**.
- KM2 coil is fed through **KM1 21-22**.

When KM1 is in, its 21-22 is open, so KM2 cannot pull in, whatever button is pressed. This is the electrical [[interlock]].

cards.title: The mechanical interlock
cards.text:
Reversing contactor pairs are usually fitted with a **mechanical interlock**: a lever between them that physically stops both closing. It still works if an auxiliary contact welds or a wire is wrong.

Good practice uses **both** interlocks. Neither one is a reason to leave out the other.

cards.title: Stop before reversing
cards.text:
In this circuit you must press STOP before changing direction, because the running contactor's holding contact keeps it in.

Reversing a motor at full speed (plugging) draws a very high current and gives the gearbox and belts a hard shock. Some machines need a short delay so the motor stops before it reverses.

cards.title: Overload and TRIP lamp
cards.text:
One overload F2 after both contactors protects the motor in both directions. Its 95-96 contact sits in series before both coil circuits, so a trip drops out whichever contactor is in. Contact 97-98 lights TRIP lamp H1.

As before, resetting the overload must not restart the motor.

show.intro: This reversing starter is wired correctly. Watch the interlocks at work in the event log.

tasks.text: Press **FORWARD (S1)**. KM1 pulls in and the motor runs forward (⟳).
While it runs forward, press and hold **REVERSE (S2)**. Nothing happens: KM1 21-22 is open, so the KM2 coil gets no supply.
Measure across **KM1 21-22** in V=. It reads 24 V: the open interlock contact is what blocks KM2.
Release S2 and press **STOP (S0)**. The motor coasts down.
Press **REVERSE (S2)**. KM2 pulls in and the motor runs in reverse (⟲).
Press **TEST** on F2. KM2 drops out and TRIP lamp H1 lights. Then press RESET: the motor does not restart.

checks.fail: KM1 and KM2 were both energised at the same time. That joins two phases: a short circuit. Each coil needs the other contactor's NC contact 21-22 in series with it.
A protective device tripped as soon as power was applied. Look for a wire joining two different phases, or + to 0 V.
The circuit will not settle (relay chatter). Check that no coil switches off its own supply.
The 24 V supply G1 is off. Check the feed from Q1 through F1 to G1.
KM1 pulls in without anyone pressing FORWARD.
KM2 pulls in without anyone pressing REVERSE.
Pressing and releasing FORWARD (S1) does not pull in and hold KM1. Trace G1 + through S0, F2 95-96, S1 (with KM1 13-14 in parallel) and KM2 21-22 to KM1 A1, then A2 to 0 V.
With KM1 in, the motor does not run forward. Check the KM1 power wiring and F2 to U1, V1, W1.
While running forward, pressing REVERSE pulled in KM2. KM1 21-22 must be in series with the KM2 coil so reverse is blocked.
STOP (S0) does not drop out KM1.
Pressing and releasing REVERSE (S2) does not pull in and hold KM2. Trace through S2 (with KM2 13-14 in parallel) and KM1 21-22 to KM2 A1.
With KM2 in, the motor does not run in reverse. KM2 must swap two phases compared with KM1 (here L1 and L3).
While running in reverse, pressing FORWARD pulled in KM1. KM2 21-22 must be in series with the KM1 coil.
An overload trip does not stop the motor. F2 95-96 must be in series with both coil circuits.
The TRIP lamp H1 does not light when F2 trips.
After resetting F2 the motor restarted by itself. It must need a new START press.
A protective device tripped during the test.

guided.intro: The power circuit and the 24 V supply are wired. **Wire the control circuit**: both direction buttons, both holding contacts, both interlocks and both coils.
hints: From F2 96, feed both direction buttons: F2:96 to S1:13 and F2:96 to S2:13.
Holding contacts in parallel with each button: S1:13 to KM1:13 and S1:14 to KM1:14; S2:13 to KM2:13 and S2:14 to KM2:14.
Forward path: S1:14 to KM2:21 (the REVERSE contactor's NC), then KM2:22 to KM1:A1.
Reverse path: S2:14 to KM1:21, then KM1:22 to KM2:A1.
Both A2 terminals return to G1 − (0 V).

unguided.intro: Now wire the **reverse contactor power wiring** (with the phase swap) and the **whole control circuit**, with no hints.

break.intro: This reversing starter has **one hidden fault**. Try both directions, then find the cause by measuring. In this simulator you may measure voltage with the power on. On a real panel, live testing is only allowed when it is justified, by a competent person, following the site risk assessment and GS38. Switch off Q1 before any Ω test.

faults.report: KM1 interlock contact 21-22 is welded closed: reverse is no longer blocked while running forward.
The KM2 coil is open circuit.
Forward holding contact KM1 13-14 does not close.
KM2 main pole 3-4 is open: reverse runs on two phases.
The wire from S2 terminal 14 to KM1 terminal 21 is broken.

extraReports: Nothing is wrong with the starter.

questions.text: How do you reverse a three-phase induction motor?
options: Swap any two of the three phases
Swap the PE and N wires
Swap all three phases round by one place
questions.explain: Swapping any two phases reverses the rotating field. Moving all three round by one place keeps the same sequence and direction.

questions.text: In a reversing starter, why is KM2 21-22 wired in series with the KM1 coil?
options: So KM1 cannot pull in while KM2 is in, which would short two phases
questions.explain: This is the electrical interlock. KM1 and KM2 together would join two phases through the contactors.

questions.text: What happens if KM1 and KM2 close together?
options: Two phases are joined: a short circuit, an arc and a trip
The motor runs at half speed
questions.explain: The joined outputs carry two different phases. The overload does not prevent a short; the short-circuit protection trips, often with damage.

questions.text: Why use a mechanical interlock as well as the electrical one?
options: It still stops both contactors closing if an auxiliary contact welds or a wire is wrong
It makes the motor reverse faster
questions.explain: Two different kinds of protection: one failure does not lead to a short.

questions.text: Why must you press STOP before reversing in this circuit, and why is that good?
options: The holding contact keeps the running contactor in; it also avoids reversing at full speed
questions.explain: Reversing at speed (plugging) gives a very high current and mechanical shock.

questions.text: The motor runs forward correctly but runs forward again when you press REVERSE. What is the likely cause?
options: The KM2 power wiring does not swap two phases
questions.explain: Reverse only works if KM2 swaps two phases compared with KM1.

questions.text: Where is the overload in a reversing starter?
options: One overload after both contactors, protecting both directions
One for each direction, before the contactors
questions.explain: Both contactor outputs feed the same overload, so the motor is protected in both directions.

questions.text: You need to correct swapped phases in the power wiring. What must you do first?
options: Isolate, lock off and prove dead
Hold the contactor in by hand
questions.explain: Power wiring is at 400 V. STOP and F1 do not isolate it.

apply.intro: Do this on the training bench while your trainer watches. Your trainer signs it off. An app score alone never makes anyone competent or authorised.

items.text: Carries out safe isolation before starting work.
Wires both contactors with the correct phase swap, a single overload, and the electrical interlocks, to the drawing.
Fits the mechanical interlock between the contactors (where supplied) and checks it moves freely.
Before energising, carries out continuity and insulation resistance tests and records them.
Functional test with the trainer: forward, reverse, STOP, each interlock blocks the other direction, overload trip, no automatic restart.
Checks the motor turns the right way for FORWARD with the machine safe (guards on, load uncoupled where needed).
